# Game Simulation compatibility

Game Simulation is a local avatar-testing controller for Unity 2022.3 and VRChat Avatars SDK 3.10.x. It supports documented desktop inputs and selected movement behavior, while preserving Gesture Manager's parameter controls. It does not reproduce the complete VRChat client or each world's locomotion configuration.

The inherited Gesture Manager 3.9.9 does not include a player gravity, WASD or Space-jump controller. Its [Locomotion menu](https://github.com/BlackStartx/VRC-Gesture-Manager/blob/9eea5c1abcdadd4f736b1290c41033753b617a47/Scripts/Editor/Modules/Vrc3/RadialMenu.cs#L215-L223) manually changes `Grounded` and velocity parameters for animation previews. Pro's Game Simulation adds movement physics and publishes those parameters from actual motion.

## Supported controls and motion

The focused Game or Scene view accepts WASD movement, comma/period (`<`/`>`) turning, Shift running, C crouch, Z prone and grounded Space jumping. The [official desktop controls](https://docs.vrchat.com/docs/keyboard-and-mouse) establish these movement keys. C and Z toggle `Upright` between standing (`1`) and crouch (`0.6`) or prone (`0.35`); pressing the active pose key again returns to standing. These pose values come from the inspected reference implementation, rather than a published VRChat guarantee.

Default walk and strafe speeds are 2 m/s; forward/backward running is 4 m/s. Shift leaves strafe speed unchanged. Input is normalized before applying the separate forward/backward and sideways speeds. The default jump impulse is 3 m/s, independently of avatar height. These defaults follow [Player Forces](https://creators.vrchat.com/worlds/udon/players/player-forces/): the default VRCWorld prefab enables jumping with an impulse of 3, while the underlying player API defaults to 0. Worlds can change these values. Game Simulation does not load world Udon settings.

Horizontal velocity approaches its target with `Vector2.MoveTowards` at 10.5 m/s² for acceleration and deceleration. This is a reference-derived choice, not a verified client constant. Releasing movement keys decelerates normally; focus loss, input suspension and blocked avatar locomotion clear motion immediately so the avatar cannot drift while controls are unavailable.

Scene Collisions is enabled by default. Game Simulation automatically enables gravity and grounded jumping while collisions are enabled; there is no separate gravity setting. Disabling Scene Collisions also disables gravity and jumping. Collision movement and ground probes use the scene. If there is no supporting ground collider at startup, a temporary invisible 100-by-100-meter collider is created at the avatar's starting foot height. Existing ground is reused; the temporary collider is removed with the session. `Grounded` follows actual support, and velocity parameters follow actual avatar displacement, including blocked movement and jump/landing transitions.

The movement capsule aligns its collision skin with the avatar's support foot point, preserving the original standing root height on level ground. It retains the normal collision margin and physics for walls, overhead obstacles, jumping, landing and falling. This alignment changes only the temporary controller, leaving model assets and the ground transform unchanged; it is not a measured VRChat client offset.

Movement does not repeatedly write `VRMode`, `TrackingType` or `Upright`. The GM Inspector remains responsible for tracking-mode selection and manual posture. Only an explicit C/Z input changes `Upright`; stopping restores its earlier value only if this session changed it. Pose keys set parameters for the avatar's existing controller and do not supply an animation.

The default view is Scene Camera: a temporary Game-view observer camera mirrors the Scene view's position and projection settings, falling back to the previously selected camera when no Scene view is available. Observer views do not follow the avatar by default. **Follow Avatar in Observer View** can be enabled or disabled during simulation. While enabled, the Scene view's pivot and its Game-view observer camera translate by the avatar's actual displacement. With every Scene view closed, following offsets only the temporary Game-view camera; the original scene camera stays unchanged. The avatar's rotation does not rotate the observer, and the user retains manual pan, rotation and zoom. Disabling following keeps the current observer position without applying earlier movement. Stopping subtracts only the translation applied by the session, preserving manual camera changes. First- and third-person cameras retain their own avatar following.

The regular Scene Camera tool also copies the Scene camera position exactly, without its inherited one-millimeter vertical offset. When that tool is already mirroring the Scene view into Game, entering and leaving the simulation observer preserves the framing; the avatar is not moved to compensate for a camera difference. Game cameras retain their own output aspect ratio. While Game Simulation owns the displayed camera, this ordinary switch controls the simulation observer and reflects View/F5 changes. Turning it off restores the prior player-camera state, including an enabled third-person feature zoomed into first person; a newly started observer returns to first person. The regular Main Camera is not synchronized in the background during simulation, and its saved selection/preference is preserved.

Player cameras restore their own perspective projection, field of view and far clip distance after leaving an observer, rather than inheriting an orthographic Scene camera or its lens settings.

The third-person preview uses the avatar root's world X/Z and the descriptor viewpoint's transformed world Y as its orbit center. It updates that height directly from the current transform, including avatar scale and parent transforms. Descriptor X/Z offsets do not displace the center off the body axis. There is no extra vertical offset, height ratio, geometry scan, mesh bake or cached mesh-top height. First-person placement still uses the complete descriptor viewpoint. Collision avoidance starts at the same body-axis center and shortens the orbit path.

VRChat exposes configurable horizontal/vertical third-person offsets in its [Graphics settings](https://wiki.vrchat.com/wiki/Third_Person_View). Pro's descriptor-height body-axis rule follows the user's requested framing; the client offset settings and exact client orbit formula remain unsupported and unverified.

F5 toggles third-person mode in the focused Game view, replacing Pro's earlier V camera cycle. Enabling the mode from first person or the observer restores the last positive distance and enters third person. Disabling it returns to first person. F5 does not select the observer; use Scene Camera in the View selector for a free observer cursor. Mouse look and cursor capture are enabled only for the Game view's First Person and Third Person views, after clicking the view or using Resume Input and releasing control keys. Mouse look turns the avatar and adjusts its viewing pitch. Pressing Esc releases a captured mouse and suspends input. Scene Camera accepts keyboard controls while keeping the mouse free.

While third-person mode is enabled and Game-view input is captured, the wheel moves the camera closer or farther away. At zero distance, the rendered view becomes first person while the third-person feature remains enabled; scrolling backward can therefore return to third person. Disabling the feature with F5 prevents the wheel from entering third person. The Inspector distance accepts 0–6 avatar heights, with zero returning to first person. Pro changes distance by 0.25 avatar heights per scroll unit; this is tool tuning, not a documented client constant or a claim to match the client's exact zoom curve.

In captured Game-view third person, Tab enables free rotation without changing the avatar heading. Mouse yaw changes an independent camera yaw; A/D supplies avatar turning instead of strafing while that mode is active. Comma/period (`<`/`>`) rotates only the camera in that mode, independently of A/D body turning, including when pressed together. A new W/S press ends free rotation, aligns the avatar to the camera heading and moves forward/backward. Existing held W/S input does not cancel a newly entered orbit, and repeated Tab presses retain its yaw. Pitch, camera collision, zoom and jump physics continue to use the existing paths. First-person/observer transitions clear free rotation. Esc or focus loss clears captured/held input while retaining the orbit until control resumes; Scene input retains its existing WASD/turning behavior and does not consume Tab. Free-rotation A/D, W/S and comma/period behavior follows the user's desktop-client observation; no new client turn-rate measurement is claimed.

The F5, Tab and wheel controls follow [VRChat 2026.2.3](https://docs.vrchat.com/docs/vrchat-202623). Free rotation while already walking follows [2026.1.1p1](https://docs.vrchat.com/docs/copy-of-vrchat-202611); retaining the orbit on repeated Tab follows the April 16 [2026.2.1 open-beta notes](https://docs.vrchat.com/docs/vrchat-202621-open-beta). Those notes also distinguish disabled third person from an enabled feature zoomed into first person. Pro does not implement the client's Graphics offset settings or complete third-person camera behavior.

The Scene view does not capture the mouse or consume F5, Tab, V or wheel input. Alt and right/middle mouse navigation suspend avatar input, and editor wheel navigation remains available. In the Game view, wheel zoom ignores Alt/Ctrl/Cmd combinations so other controls can use them; Shift plus wheel can zoom. Shift+F5 does not toggle third-person mode, preserving gesture shortcuts. These focus and modifier rules are editor integration choices. Esc releasing input is also an editor convenience; the client's Escape Quick Menu and V microphone control are outside this tool's scope.

## GestureManager+ reference inspection

The user-supplied `GestureManager+.zip` (13,619 bytes) contains `GestureManager+/GestureManagerPlus_v1.0.0.unitypackage`. Its editor asset `Assets/GestureManagerPlus/Editor/LocomotionKeysGM.Editor.dll` is 24,576 bytes. The package also contains a Runtime assembly definition and `LocomotionKeysRunner.cs`. The archive contents and DLL metadata/IL were inspected statically on 2026-10-16; the DLL was not executed. This inspection is evidence about that package version, not a measurement of the VRChat client.

The reference DLL exposes `WALK = 2`, `RUN = 4`, `ACCEL = 10.5`, `JUMP_SPEED = 2.8` and `GRAVITY = 9.8`, uses `Vector2.MoveTowards`, and sets `Upright` to `1`, `0.6`, `0.35` or `0.2` through its standing/C/Z/X posture controls. It does not set `VRMode` or `TrackingType`. These observations informed preserving GM's tracking controls and adding acceleration and C/Z posture input.

Other reference behavior is deliberately not adopted. Its running multiplier applies across movement axes, whereas the official strafe default is unaffected by running. Its 2.8 jump speed differs from the default VRCWorld impulse of 3. It reports `Grounded` from its internal jumping state and uses requested speed for grounded `VelocityMagnitude`; Pro retains collider-based grounding and measured displacement. The reference directly translates all controlled avatars and the Scene camera; Pro keeps one owned simulation session, collision movement and an observer camera whose translation following is optional and disabled by default. X lie posture is not listed among the official desktop controls and is not added. The reference's global Editor shortcut-profile changes are not required for Pro's focused-view input handling.

No locomotion animation assets or embedded animation resources were found in the supplied reference, and no animation-generation path was identified. Its dependency on the original Gesture Manager does not supply the VRChat client's animation replacement. No reference DLL or implementation code is copied into this package.

## Animation and client limitations

The SDK locomotion proxy clips inspected for this work have zero duration and do not contain a looping gait. The [VRChat proxy animation documentation](https://creators.vrchat.com/avatars/#proxy-animations) explains that the client replaces recognized `proxy_` animations with built-in clips. Game Simulation does not implement that replacement. An avatar using those SDK proxies can move and receive velocity/posture parameters while its limbs remain static in the editor. Its actual custom locomotion clips can still be evaluated by the inherited simulator. The package does not generate substitute walks, runs, crouches or prone animations to conceal missing client functionality.

First-person rendering hides the whole local avatar only for the simulation camera. Visible first-person body/arms, client head clipping, body IK, VR tracking and calibration are unsupported. AngularY scaling, collision details, world-specific locomotion, networking and client audio behavior are not established as equivalent to VRChat. Check final animation and movement behavior using the SDK's local Build & Test in the client. Static reference inspection and automated editor checks do not replace that comparison or physical input and avatar validation.
